title: Chapter 2: Managed vs Self-Managed: The Real Tradeoffs

questions.q: Which statement accurately describes the RDS for SQL Server master user?
options: It is a full sysadmin with OS access
It is not a full sysadmin — it manages logins and databases but cannot grant itself server-level permissions AWS reserves
It is identical to Azure SQL's db_owner role
It can SSH into the underlying EC2 host
questions.explain: The chapter emphasizes the master user is not full sysadmin: it cannot grant itself server-level permissions AWS reserves or touch the OS, so sysadmin-dependent tooling like xp_cmdshell scripts needs redesign.

questions.q: What happens when you perform a point-in-time restore on RDS, Azure SQL, or Cloud SQL?
options: The existing instance is overwritten in place
Only the transaction log is replayed onto the live database
A new database instance is always created; you must redirect traffic to the new endpoint
The restore pauses the primary for the duration of the replay
questions.explain: The chapter states PITR restores always create a new DB instance rather than overwriting the existing one, so recovery procedures must account for provisioning time and connection redirection.

questions.q: Which storage statement matches the chapter's Terraform guidance for RDS?
options: gp2 is the recommended default for new deployments
Magnetic storage is fine for reporting workloads
gp3 replaced gp2 as the default: 3000 baseline IOPS and 125 MB/s regardless of volume size, with independent scaling
io1 is always cheaper than gp3 for OLTP
questions.explain: The chapter states gp3 replaced gp2 as the default general-purpose type, providing 3000 baseline IOPS and 125 MB/s independent of volume size, and gp2 should not be used for new deployments.

questions.q: You modify a static parameter (e.g., max server memory) in the parameter group of a Multi-AZ RDS instance. What happens?
options: The change applies to the primary only; the standby is unaffected
The change is rejected until you fail over manually
The change applies immediately with no reboot
The pending reboot applies to both primary and standby — treat it with the care of a planned failover
questions.explain: The chapter warns that on Multi-AZ, a static parameter change applies to both primary and standby during the next maintenance window (or immediately if forced), effectively acting as a planned failover.

questions.q: After a Multi-AZ failover, what does the DBA still own?
options: Rewriting the RDS DNS endpoint manually
Patching the standby's OS
Application reconnection logic, because the endpoint DNS changes and client-side DNS caching can hold stale entries for minutes
Rebuilding the synchronous replication topology
questions.explain: RDS failover changes the IP behind the DNS endpoint (TTL 5 seconds), but JVMs, connection poolers, and OS resolvers can cache stale entries — application reconnection logic is the DBA/app boundary the managed service does not cover.
